questionStem: A 62-year-old woman has shortness of breath immediately after beginning transfusion of fresh frozen plasma and 2 units of packed red blood cells to manage acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding. She has been hospitalized for 24 hours. Five years ago, she underwent mechanical valve replacement for treatment of aortic stenosis. She has no other history of serious illness. Her only outpatient medications are warfarin and lisinopril, which have been discontinued since admission. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 110/min and regular, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 82%. Crackles are heard from the lung bases to the midlung fields. There is cyanosis of the upper and lower extremities. A urinary catheter is draining clear urine. A chest x-ray is pending. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with sudden onset dyspnea, hypoxia, and fever following transfusion of packed red blood cells and plasma. TRALI is a syndrome characterized by respiratory distress, often with associated hypoxemia, cyanosis, fever, and new infiltrates on chest x-ray, that develops within 6 hours of transfusion of any blood product, including erythrocytes, fresh frozen plasma, or platelets. Frequently, symptoms develop within minutes to hours after starting transfusion. The pathogenesis of TRALI is thought to involve abnormal priming of neutrophils in the lung, which, when exposed to inflammatory cytokines present in transfused blood products, undergo widespread activation within the lung parenchyma. Release of cytokines and reactive oxygen species among other inflammatory components from activated neutrophils causes endothelial dysfunction and rapidly leads to non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. This contrasts with the pulmonary edema that develops in patients who develop respiratory failure secondary to transfusion associated cardiac overload (TACO). Treatment is with supportive care, which may include implementing non-invasive or invasive ventilation, vasopressors, and antipyretics. Importantly, patients who recover from TRALI can receive additional blood products, but these products should not be from the same prior blood donor.

questionStem: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 50 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision. He was an unrestrained passenger. On arrival, he is alert. He says he has neck pain and numbness in both legs; he cannot move his legs. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 70/min, respirations are 20/min and unlabored, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg. Examination shows a patent airway. There is no jugular venous distention. There are multiple contusions over the trunk and a bony deformity of the right calf. The cervical spine is tender. Sensation to touch is absent below the midchest. Abdominal ultrasonography for trauma (FAST) shows no free fluid in the pelvis. X-rays of the cervical spine show subluxation of C7 on T1. X-rays of the chest and pelvis show no abnormalities. An x-ray of the right lower extremity shows comminuted fractures of the tibia and fibula. CT scans of the abdomen and pelvis show a small contained hematoma. Loss of sympathetic innervation results in vasodilation and loss of vascular tone. Disruption of sympathetic fibers descending from the cardiovascular center in the medulla oblongata may also lead to bradycardia. Careful fluid resuscitation is essential for maintaining perfusion. Atropine may be trialed for the management of bradycardia following acute traumatic spinal cord injury, and vasoactive infusions such as norepinephrine may be necessary to maintain perfusion. Competing diagnoses such as blood loss in the setting of trauma must be excluded or managed if present.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 3-week history of headache. The headache has worsened today and is now accompanied by mildly blurred vision. Her mother has a history of migraines. The patient is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 91 kg (200 Ib); BMI is 34 kg/m2. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 76/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Funduscopic examination shows bilateral papilledema. Headaches that are secondary to increased intracranial pressure often worsen when lying down and are relieved by standing. The most common risk factors for the development of IIH include female sex and obesity. Medications associated with IIH include tetracyclines, danazol, and growth hormone. CT scan is an important initial step in the evaluation of a patient with papilledema and suspected IIH to exclude the presence of an intracranial mass. If the CT scan is normal, lumbar puncture is the most appropriate next step to confirm the presence of increased intracranial pressure. Management of IIH includes weight reduction, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, therapeutic lumbar puncture, and in rare cases, surgical intervention with cerebrospinal fluid shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration.

Intravenous administration of methylprednisolone (Choice B) is useful for the acute management of optic neuritis, which generally presents with acute onset vision loss and ocular pain that is exacerbated with extraocular movements. questionStem: A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after rescue workers found him on a snow-covered mountain. At the scene, he was alert and oriented but shivering and unable to walk without assistance. He said he had become lost while cross-country skiing. On arrival, he is shivering and reports that his toes are numb. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 60/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 120/65 mm Hg. Examination shows pale toes bilaterally. Blisters are noted on the 4th and 5th toes bilaterally. Sensation to touch is absent over the toes bilaterally. Pedal pulses are faintly palpable in both feet. Ankle brachial indices are 0.85 bilaterally (N>1). Tetanus toxoid is administered, and the feet are immersed in a 104°F water bath for 20 minutes. During immersion, his feet become painful. In addition to administration of acetaminophen, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

There are several ways to classify the severity of frostbite, depending on degree of cyanosis, depth of tissue involvement, blistering, or findings on technetium-99m imaging. Immediate management of frostbite involves removing cold or wet clothing, transferring the patient to a warm environment, rapid rewarming by immersing the affected area in warm (but not hot) water, analgesia, and admission to the hospital for observation and wound care. Several adjunct therapies are often employed to limit tissue damage, including thrombolysis. Initial signs and symptoms of frostbite are often unreliable in determining the extent of injury; the clinical picture evolves as occult damage becomes apparent.

questionStem: An 87-year-old man is transferred to the hospital from a skilled nursing care facility 6 hours after staff noticed black skin on his right leg. He has had three strokes during the past 2 years. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Current medications include metoprolol, glipizide, and clopidogrel. He does not smoke. He is not communicative and responds only to painful stimuli. There are severe contractures of the lower extremities. Examination of the lower extremities shows black skin over the right ankle and foot. Pulses are absent in the lower extremities distally. Extension of the hips is limited to 110 degrees; extension of the knees is limited to 70 degrees. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) refers to the abnormally diminished flow of blood to the extremities secondary to atherosclerotic plaque. This most commonly affects the lower extremities. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, increased age, tobacco smoking, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. A known history of atherosclerosis (eg, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease) identifies the likelihood of the condition being present in other locations as well. Patients with PAD typically present with intermittent claudication, which results from insufficient blood flow to the muscles during exercise. As the flow of blood becomes progressively diminished with worsening atherosclerosis, tissue perfusion may become inadequate to meet metabolic demands, and can present with pain at rest and the potential for ischemia and necrosis (gangrene) of the extremity. Dry gangrene is most common in patients with PAD, although wet gangrene may also occur. Revascularization surgery may allow for salvage of the limb and improve rest pain or non-healing wounds, but the presence of gangrene generally requires amputation. In this case, an immobile patient with contractures will generally not suffer functional loss from amputation, making it a suitable choice if it aligns with goals of care.

questionStem: A 62-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. She does not smoke and only drinks socially. A systolic ejection murmur is best heard over the second right intercostal space with transmission to the carotid arteries. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm and a pattern of left ventricular hypertrophy with strain. Which of the following manifestations would indicate the need for aortic valve replacement?
correctExplanation: Aortic stenosis (AS) is a common disorder of the aortic valve that results from calcification. Calcification of the aortic valve is a pathologic consequence of mechanical stresses on heart valves, and results from repetitive microtrauma from the opening and closing of valve leaflets with associated chronic inflammation. While many patients may be asymptomatic, those with severe AS may complain of fatigue, shortness of breath, cough, diminished exercise tolerance, angina, or syncope with exertion. Due to the chronic increased afterload from a fixed obstruction by the valve, left ventricular hypertrophy and resultant diastolic dysfunction can occur. If untreated, complications of aortic stenosis include heart failure, secondary pulmonary hypertension, and potential sudden cardiac death. Angina and syncope result from inadequate end-organ perfusion (of the myocardium and brain respectively), and the presence of these symptoms in the setting of AS is an indication for aortic valve replacement.

Pulmonary embolus (Choice D) is not directly associated with aortic stenosis, although the stenotic valve can potentially cause increased left ventricular strain, pulmonary congestion, and impaired systemic perfusion. While the distinction of provoked or unprovoked DVT matters in deciding long-term anticoagulation, in the immediate setting, the management is the same regardless of the reason for occurrence, and anticoagulation is the appropriate best next step. Recent surgery may be considered a relative contraindication to anticoagulation, and a careful assessment of bleeding risk should be performed. Clinical calculators, such as the HAS-BLED score, can be useful for quantifying the risk of bleeding with anticoagulation. questionStem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 6-month history of intermittent bright red rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy often discloses numerous polyps, but the histology is characteristic and sets JPS apart from many other polyposis syndromes. Polyps in JPS may be of many different varieties, but the most common type are called hamartomas. Hamartomatous polyps are made up of various tissues within the gastrointestinal tract, and histologically, they have inflammatory cells within the lamina propria in addition to mucin-filled, dilated glands. Other associated findings include telangiectasias of the skin, the gastrointestinal tract, the liver, and the lungs. He drinks coffee with dinner. He does not smoke. Examination shows no abnormalities. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The most appropriate next step in management is esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). Mild epigastric pain and nausea after eating is commonly caused by gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD); however, this patient also has occult blood in the stool. Evidence of a gastrointestinal bleed (melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, positive occult blood in stool, unexplained iron deficiency anemia) with these symptoms is an indication for EGD to rule out malignancy. Unexplained weight loss, anorexia, progressive dysphagia, and a first-degree relative with cancer are additional red flags. EGD can rule out additional diagnoses, such as esophagitis, and collect biopsy samples at the time of the procedure. Biopsy samples may look for Helicobacter pylori infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disorders.

However, the patient needs further workup to identify the etiology of his symptoms. Serum Helicobacter pylori antibody assay (Choice B) is not commonly used, as serology cannot distinguish between an active or past infection. Urea breath testing or stool antigen testing may be useful if the initial EGD and biopsy are nondiagnostic. Upper gastrointestinal series (Choice C) should be performed prior to an EGD for patients at risk of esophageal perforation. questionStem: A 53-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of increasingly severe abdominal cramping and malaise. She has a 3-year history of ulcerative pancolitis, treated with sulfasalazine. Four days ago she had hematochezia and an increase in the frequency and volume of bowel movements; treatment with prednisone resulted in no significant improvement. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows moderate distention, diminished bowel sounds, and diffuse tenderness without rigidity on palpation. Supine and erect x-rays of the abdomen show gas distending the colon. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.A: Carcinoma of the colon with obstruction
choices.B: Dysplasia of the colon with hemorrhage

correctExplanation: This patient’s presentation is highly concerning for toxic megacolon, a rare but known complication of ulcerative colitis. Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening medical emergency caused by extensive inflammation of the colon. The classic constellation of clinical manifestations includes high fever, tachycardia, hypotension, leukocytosis, enlarged and dilated bowel, and impaired colonic motility. More generally, ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory condition within the spectrum of inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulcers of the colonic mucosa, typically beginning with the rectum and advancing proximally. Symptoms include chronic abdominal pain, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and tenesmus. Extraintestinal manifestations such as uveitis also occur. In addition, because of the chronic inflammation of the colon, patients are at increased risk of developing colorectal carcinoma. Treatment of ulcerative colitis flares includes supportive care, immunomodulators, biologics, and steroids. In severe cases, a partial or total colectomy may be required, especially in cases of toxic megacolon.

Carcinoma of the colon with obstruction (Choice A) is another potential complication of chronic inflammatory bowel disease but is less likely to explain the patient’s current presentation. Large bowel obstruction typically presents with abdominal pain, distension, obstipation, and constipation. X-rays typically show proximal colonic dilation with a transition point at the site of the obstruction. Dysplasia of the colon with hemorrhage (Choice B), also called angiodysplasia, is a common cause of gastrointestinal bleeding and could explain the patient’s hematochezia. questionStem: A 72-year-old man who is in the hospital has had abdominal cramps and bright red rectal bleeding for the past 6 hours. During this period, he has passed three bloody, moderately sized stools. Two days ago, he underwent surgical resection of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. He had a hemorrhage during dissection of the aneurysm and had hypotension for the first 20 minutes of the operation. He received 6 units of packed red blood cells. His initial postoperative course was uncomplicated, and he was extubated within 24 hours. Current medications are intravenous cefazolin and subcutaneous heparin. His current temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and moderate left lower quadrant tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Ischemic colitis refers to insufficient blood flow to an area of the intestine and should be suspected in a patient with abdominal pain and hematochezia. It can be caused by an occlusion of the mesenteric vasculature, such as from thromboembolism or dissection, or from hypotension or limited blood flow causing a watershed infarction. Aortic surgery is a known risk factor for ischemic colitis, often because of dislodgement of endovascular plaques with subsequent embolization, or because of hypotension. Risk factors for acute ischemic colitis include older age, coronary artery disease, hypercoagulability, peripheral arterial disease, or recent endovascular surgery. Typical symptoms of patients with acute ischemic colitis include crampy abdominal pain, tenderness over the affected bowel, and hematochezia. Ischemic colitis can be complicated by necrosis, viscus perforation, or ileus. Treatment typically involves supportive care, anticoagulation, antibiotics, and surgery in cases of bowel infarction, necrosis, or perforation.

Aortoenteric fistula (Choice A) is an abnormal communication between the aorta and gastrointestinal lumen commonly caused by compression or inflammation of the aorta or bowel in proximity to each other, often in the setting of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Patients may present with gastrointestinal bleeding, which may be mild or may lead to rapid exsanguination. This patient’s history of recent surgery complicated by hypotension is more suggestive of ischemic colitis. Cecal angiodysplasia (Choice B) refers to an abnormal dilation and ectasia of a cecal blood vessel. Cecal angiodysplasia is often acquired and presents in older adults with gastrointestinal bleeding. questionStem: A 37-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of moderate rectal pain, rectal itching, and bleeding with bowel movements. She is otherwise healthy and takes no medications. On digital rectal examination, the rectal tissue is tender and inflamed. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hemorrhoids occur because of enlargement and distal displacement of the anal cushions, which are normal prominences of the anal mucosa composed of smooth muscle, vascular, and connective tissues, and play an important role in maintaining continence. Hemorrhoids may primarily involve tissue derived from the internal, superior hemorrhoidal plexus or the external, inferior hemorrhoidal plexus. Symptoms include pain with defecation, incontinence, hematochezia, and anal itching. Hemorrhoids may also undergo acute thrombosis and cause acute, often severe pain. The diagnosis is clinical and may be established with a rectal examination, which can be facilitated via anoscopy. Treatment is mainly supportive and includes a high fiber diet, sitz baths, and oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Band ligation, sclerotherapy, or surgical excision may be used for severe hemorrhoids or those that fail to improve with conservative management.

It plays no role in the evaluation of hemorrhoids. questionStem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of increasingly severe abdominal pain for the past 4 hours and a temperature of 39°C (102.2°F) and shaking chills for the past 2 hours. The pain began 1 hour after eating dinner. During the past 2 weeks, she has had 30-minute episodes of epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain after eating. Treatment with antacids sometimes relieves the pain. She now is lying still on the examination table. Her temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Examination shows scleral icterus and jaundice. Abdominal examination shows right upper quadrant tenderness to percussion and involuntary guarding; bowel sounds are normal. Urinalysis is positive for bile. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Cholelithiasis refers to the presence of a gallstone or gallstones in the gallbladder, and choledocholithiasis refers to the presence of a gallstone located within the biliary tree. Gallstones can result in varying degrees of obstruction, which dictates the severity of presenting symptoms. Cholelithiasis can result in colicky right upper quadrant or epigastric pain (biliary colic), nausea, or vomiting; with obstructive choledocholithiasis, increased direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase may be present on laboratory assay, along with persistent, non-colicky discomfort on examination. Hyperbilirubinemia can lead to scleral icterus and jaundice. Depending on the location of the bile duct stone, choledocholithiasis can result in acute pancreatitis, which manifests with epigastric pain and increased pancreatic enzymes (amylase, lipase). Acute cholangitis occurs secondary to acute bacterial infection of the biliary tree, typically in the setting of biliary instrumentation or choledocholithiasis as a precursor. Cholangitis describes a bacterial infection or inflammation of the biliary tree, and commonly presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice (Charcot triad), along with possible shock and altered mental status (Reynold pentad). Treatment includes fluid resuscitation, antibiotic therapy, and procedural intervention to clear any obstruction and permit drainage of infection.

questionStem: A 57-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of increasingly severe left-sided chest pain that is worse when she inhales. Six hours ago, she underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy because of a 1-month history of progressive dysphagia. Results showed a benign-appearing stricture of the distal esophagus that was balloon-dilated. Her only medication is esomeprazole for gastroesophageal reflux disease. She does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. She appears anxious. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.3°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg. Examination shows splinting of the left chest during inspiration. Cardiac examination shows a regular tachycardia. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Chest x-ray shows a small left pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Upper endoscopy is a generally safe procedure, though complications can include bleeding, aspiration, and perforation; depending on the purpose of the endoscopy, specific complications such as pancreatitis following endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) can occur. In the case of dysphagia in this patient, the endoscopy was performed and dilated an esophageal stricture to promote passage of food bolus. Stretching of smooth muscle, stricture, and connective tissue, especially if chronic inflammation has resulted in compromise of the stromal strength of the esophageal wall, can lead to perforation. A perforated esophagus is diagnosed on water-soluble contrast esophagography. An esophageal perforation permits translocation of gastrointestinal contents such as food, stomach acid, and bacteria into the mediastinum, which can lead to fatal mediastinitis if untreated. Mediastinitis can present with chest pain and a generally toxic appearance (eg, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis). Management of esophageal perforation is through antibiotics and emergent surgical intervention.

It can also identify intrathoracic fluid collections that may require drainage. However, water-soluble contrast esophagography is the best first step in diagnosis. questionStem: A 25-year-old man has postoperative pain 6 hours after a mesh repair of an inguinal hernia under local (lidocaine) anesthesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate analgesic pharmacotherapy for the incisional pain?

choices.D: F ) Infiltration of the wound with bupivacaine

correctExplanation: Incisional pain after an abdominal surgery can be moderate to severe and typically lasts for days to weeks. Oral administration of non-opiate medications may be helpful for pain control, but many patients may require opioid analgesics to control severe pain. Typically, the approach to adequately controlling pain is multimodal. While opioid medications can offer strong analgesia, opiates are central nervous system depressants and can lead to dependence, addiction, and death. Opiate intoxication causes sedation, bradycardia and hypotension, depressed respiratory drive, and constricted pupils. Opiates are commonly used for analgesia and act on receptors within the gastrointestinal tract, reducing gut motility and thus causing constipation. Adjunctive pain medications, such as acetaminophen, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications, gabapentin, and others, can help reduce the use of opiate medications and reduce the risk for its side effects, tolerance, and dependence. Short-term therapy following surgery with opiate compounds is indicated, though care should be taken to avoid prolonged use due to the risk of side effects and dependence.

It also can affect bleeding, clotting, and healing, so would not be the first choice for analgesia in a postoperative patient. questionStem: A 5-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-week history of progressive jaundice. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. His mother says that his stools are white. He is at the 50th percentiles for height and weight. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F). Examination shows moderate jaundice. The liver edge is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin and is firm and slightly nodular. Serum studies show: Bilirubin, total 12.4 mg/dL Direct 8.3 mg/dL Alkaline phosphatase 551 U/L AST 51 U/L ALT 48 U/L a.-Antitrypsin normal A TORCH assay is negative. An ultrasonography of the abdomen does not show a gallbladder. A technetium 99m scan shows prompt uptake throughout the liver and no gallbladder; no tracer appears in the bowel. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's jaundice?
correctExplanation: In congenital biliary atresia, the common bile duct is occluded, diminutive, or absent, and bile is unable to pass into the duodenum. This precludes the use of bile in the digestion of dietary fats and causes fat malabsorption. In contrast to benign causes of neonatal jaundice, biliary atresia presents with progressively worsening jaundice (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia), pale stools, dark urine, poor weight gain, and, in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension. Classically, benign etiologies of neonatal jaundice will improve by the second to third week of life, whereas biliary atresia will persist and often worsen within the first 8 weeks of life. Diagnosis consists of history and physical examination, liver function testing, HIDA scan or cholangiography, with definitive diagnosis occurring during exploratory surgery with visualization of atretic bile ducts. Treatment is through hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai procedure), which restores biliary flow, reduces jaundice, and helps salvage the native liver function. Liver transplant may be required if the procedure is unsuccessful. ¢ G E 6 o Lab Values Calculator Help Pause Score Report starttest.com

questionStem: Twenty-four hours after undergoing splenectomy for trauma sustained in a motor vehicle collision, a previously healthy 25-year-old woman has oliguria. A urinary catheter is in place, and her urine output has been 20 mL/h during the past 3 hours. Intraoperative complications included a 30-minute period of hypotension and a total blood loss of 2.5 L requiring 4 units of packed red blood cells. Currently, her temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation, and breath sounds are heard bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows no distention. Bowel sounds are absent. Laboratory studies show a hematocrit of 28%, serum urea nitrogen concentration of 30 mg/dL, and serum creatinine concentration of 2.5 mg/dL; her serum electrolyte concentrations are within the reference ranges. Central venous pressure is 8 cm H,O (N=5-8). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the cause of the oliguria?

choices.B: Measurement of plasma free hemoglobin concentration

correctExplanation: Acute kidney injury is defined as an acute increase in creatinine by greater than or equal to 0.3 mg/dL or 1.5 times above baseline creatinine, occasionally with oliguria or anuria. Acute kidney injury can be prerenal (because of dehydration, low vascular perfusion states such as congestive heart failure, or intrinsic such as acute tubular necrosis) or postrenal because of obstruction. A common cause is acute tubular necrosis, which can be caused by ischemia in the setting of prolonged hypoperfusion or toxins. A way to distinguish between the causes of acute kidney injury is by measuring the fractional excretion of sodium. The fractional excretion of a solute measures the percentage of the original filtered amount that is present in the excreted urine. The calculations are made using the plasma and urine concentrations of the sodium and creatinine. Prerenal and intrinsic kidney injury can be distinguished by the fractional excretion of sodium, which is <1% in prerenal and >2% in intrinsic kidney injury. In acute tubular necrosis, laboratory evaluation will show a blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio of less than 20, a fractional excretion of sodium greater than 2%, and muddy brown casts on urinalysis.

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that serves as an aldosterone receptor antagonist. It would not be appropriate to start a diuretic before diagnosing the cause of acute kidney injury, as it can exacerbate the kidney injury. questionStem: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after sustaining extensive injuries in a motor vehicle collision. His pulse is 100/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. The lower abdomen is tender. There is blood at the urethral meatus. On rectal examination, the prostate is not palpable, and there is no blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of the urinary tract?
correctExplanation: A patient with pelvic injury and blood at the urethral meatus raises suspicion for a urethral injury. Urethral injuries are characterized by difficulty voiding, blood at the urethral meatus, perineal ecchymosis, and may be associated with a pelvic fracture. Straddle injuries can cause trauma to the anterior urethra, while pelvic fractures may injure the posterior urethra. Urethral injuries are evaluated by retrograde urethrography, which involves the injection of contrast into the urethra to evaluate for the extravasation of contrast, indicating urethral discontinuity. Depending on the location and severity of urethral injury, patients may require surgical repair or the placement of a urethral catheter to help promote healing and prevent complications of urinary extravasation, infection, urethrocutaneous fistula, or urethral stricture.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Cystography (Choice A) is indicated for evaluation of the urinary bladder when a bladder injury is suspected. This allows for characterization of an intraperitoneal versus extraperitoneal bladder rupture, but it would not be the best first choice in suspected urethral injury. Intravenous pyelography (Choice B) involves the intravenous injection of radiopaque contrast to subsequently visualize the kidney collecting system, ureters, and bladder under fluoroscopy. This allows for the investigation of suspected urinary tract anatomic abnormalities, malignancies, obstruction, malformation, and strictures. Ultrasonography of the pelvis (Choice D) such as that performed in a focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) examination would be able to identify free peritoneal fluid; similarly, a CT scan of the pelvis (Choice E) can identify solid organ injury and the presence of free fluid, but neither would be able to directly identify a urethral injury. ¢ G € 6 t Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause starttest.com

questionStem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of bloody discharge from the right nipple for 2 weeks. There are no breast masses or axillary or supraclavicular adenopathy. Mammography shows normal findings. The nipple and areola appear normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The most common cause of unilateral bloody nipple discharge is an intraductal papilloma, which may be associated with focal ductal carcinoma in situ. However, an intraductal papilloma itself is a benign lesion. Nipple discharge may be caused by lactation, physiologic mechanisms such as galactorrhea, or pathologic lesions such as breast cancer or infection. Evaluation includes a careful history and physical examination, with particular attention paid to whether the discharge is unilateral or bilateral, if it is from a single or multiple ducts, and whether it is associated with any breast abnormalities (eg, skin changes, breast lumps). Lactation and physiologic discharge are more commonly bilateral and from multiple ducts, whereas pathological lesions more commonly present unilaterally. Further diagnostic evaluation of pathologic discharge, as in this patient, often involves ultrasonography or mammography based on patient age. If an abnormality is detected, biopsy is recommended.

However, this patient's mammography showed normal findings, making breast cancer such as ductal carcinoma in situ unlikely. Fibroadenoma (Choice B) is a well-circumscribed, mobile breast mass generally seen in women of reproductive age. Mammography or ultrasonography would show a solid mass. Fibroadenomas do not routinely present with nipple discharge. Paget disease of the breast (Choice D) describes skin changes of the nipple and areola that are often related to underlying malignancy. These skin changes include discoloration, erythema, and ulceration. questionStem: A previously healthy 42-year-old woman comes to the office because of a painful mass in the right breast for 3 weeks. Menarche was at the age of 12 years. She had her first child at the age of 22 years. Examination shows a 1-cm, firm, tender mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast; there is no lymphadenopathy. Examination of a biopsy specimen shows fibroadenoma and lobular carcinoma in situ. Over the next 10 years, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
correctExplanation: Breast masses are common in women, and breast cancer is the most common non-dermatologic malignancy in women. Evaluation of a new breast mass includes a thorough history and physical examination. Benign masses are commonly small, well-circumscribed, and mobile, whereas malignant lesions are more likely to be large, poorly defined, adherent to underlying tissue, and associated with skin or nipple changes. Although a significant portion of breast masses are benign, they may be associated with future malignancy. However, it is associated with an increase in the risk of development of invasive breast carcinoma, which may occur in either the ipsilateral or contralateral breast, although it is not considered a precursor lesion. Therefore, this patient is at greatest risk for developing invasive ductal carcinoma in the next 10 years. questionStem: A previously healthy 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after falling 12 feet from a barn loft. He landed straddling a wooden beam. His pulse is 120/min; other vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the scrotum and penis shows edema and ecchymoses. Urinalysis shows numerous RBCs. Doppler ultrasonography of the testes shows a scrotal hematoma; there is no blood flow to the testes. An analgesic is administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Blunt trauma of the external genitalia in a male can lead to injury to the testes, penis, and anterior urethra. Specifically, blunt trauma to the penis can result in penile fracture, whereas trauma to the scrotum can cause rupture of the testes, vascular injury, and testicular torsion and hematoma. A straddle injury, as in this patient, causes injury to the perineum with subsequent disruption of the bulbar urethra. Penile fractures result with pain, edema, and ecchymoses, whereas testicular rupture or vascular injury presents with testicular swelling and ecchymoses, with disruption of the testicular anatomy. Disruption of the bulbar urethra presents with hematuria on urinalysis. This patient has many genitourinary abnormalities following his straddle injury, including a possible penile fracture, scrotal hematoma, and possible testicular vascular injury and urethral injury. The absence of blood flow to the testes is a surgical emergency and requires prompt evaluation by surgical exploration to try to restore blood flow and prevent testicular necrosis and resultant infertility. The next most appropriate step in management of this patient is surgical exploration.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Renal ultrasonography (Choice A) may be used to evaluate the kidney if there was suspicion of upper genitourinary tract injury. questionStem: Twenty-four hours after undergoing total thyroidectomy and lymph node dissection for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma, a 57-year-old woman has circumoral paresthesia and tingling of the fingertips. Examination shows hyperreflexia when the facial nerve is tapped. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

The parathyroid glands are located along the posterior aspect of the thyroid gland and, while not frequent, can sometimes be inadvertently removed during a thyroidectomy. The parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH), which has numerous actions, including the stimulation of vitamin D activation in the kidneys and resorption of calcium from the bones to maintain calcium homeostasis. questionStem: Two days after undergoing thoracotomy for a stab wound to the right hemithorax, a 25-year-old woman has oliguria despite adequate fluid replacement. During the operation, she received 4 units of packed red blood cells. Her hematocrit is 35%, serum urea nitrogen concentration is 12 mg/dL, and serum creatinine concentration is 0.9 mg/dL. Her oliguria is most likely caused by an increased concentration of which of the following hormones?
correctExplanation: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin, ADH) is a hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary that leads to water reabsorption in the collecting duct of the renal tubule by increasing the amount of aquaporin channels. It also increases systemic vascular resistance by causing peripheral vasoconstriction and consequently increases blood pressure. Its secretion is stimulated by increased plasma osmolality and decreased arterial blood volume. The syndrome of inappropriate secretion of ADH (SIADH) occurs when ADH is secreted independently of plasma osmolality or arterial blood volume. This most commonly occurs in neurologic injury, as a medication side effect, or because of ectopic production by a malignant tumor or lung disease. However, surgery can also cause an increase in secretion of ADH, thought to be secondary to pain. Inappropriate secretion of ADH in relation to plasma osmolality and blood volume results in decreased urine output; when this occurs, the residual urine is concentrated, with urine studies showing a urine osmolality above 100 mOsmol/kg and urine sodium above 40 mEq/L. While hypovolemia or obstruction can cause oliguria, these would likely also increase the patient’s serum urea nitrogen and creatinine. As these parameters are normal, this patient's oliguria is most likely secondary to an increased concentration of ADH.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cortisol (Choice B) is increased in Cushing syndrome, which presents with hypertension, central adiposity, moon facies, hirsutism, striae, proximal muscle weakness, and insulin resistance. This can be caused by Cushing disease, exogenous glucocorticoids, or a variety of other etiologies. However, Cushing syndrome more commonly presents with polyuria than oliguria. Epinephrine (Choice C) and norepinephrine (Choice E) excess would be expected to present with signs of sympathetic nervous system activation, such as tachycardia and hypertension. This consequently would lead to increased cardiac output and theoretically increased renal perfusion, which may be associated with increased rather than decreased urine output. questionStem: Eight hours after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, an obese 55-year-old man has a pulse of 150/min and blood pressure of 60/40 mm Hg. Hematocrit is 28% (42% preoperatively). Serum creatine kinase activity is 200 U/L. MB isoenzyme of creatine kinase fraction is less than 2% (N<5% of total). Arterial Po, is 70 mm Hg. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia without other changes. Central venous pressure is 2 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Sudden postoperative hypotension is presumed to be caused by bleeding until determined otherwise. Other causes of postoperative hypotension include under-resuscitation during the procedure, medication side effects, and sepsis. Hypovolemia, whether due to anemia or fluid depletion, results in a compensatory tachycardia to try to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP). However, with significant enough hypovolemia, the tachycardia is unable to maintain the MAP, the blood pressure subsequently falls, and the patient becomes hypotensive. Other evidence of postoperative bleeding in this patient includes a decrease in hematocrit from 42% to 28% (although a decrease in hematocrit may not always be present with an acute bleed), and a low central venous pressure indicating hypovolemia. Other signs of bleeding include pallor and swelling or ecchymoses of the surgical site. Management of postoperative hypotension caused by bleeding includes fluid resuscitation, blood product transfusion, pressor therapy, and prompt surgical re-exploration.

Adrenal insufficiency (depending on level — primary, secondary, tertiary) presents variably with weight loss, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Patients with Addison disease may develop an Addisonian crisis in response to a variety of stressors, such as severe infection or a surgical procedure. This often presents with lethargy, confusion, and hypotension. This patient has no other symptoms of Addison disease but does have a decreased central venous pressure and hematocrit, making postoperative bleeding a more likely cause of this patient's hypotension. questionStem: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision. He was the unrestrained driver. On arrival, he is oriented to person but not to place or time. He has no documentation in his wallet regarding his religious affiliation, but his friend says she thinks he might be a Jehovah's Witness. His family cannot be contacted. questionStem: A 37-year-old woman remains ventilator-dependent 3 weeks after undergoing a gastric restrictive procedure. She has obstructive sleep apnea and restrictive lung disease. Preoperative arterial blood gas analysis on room air showed a pH of 7.35, PCO, of 65 mm Hg, and Po, of 45 mm Hg. She is currently receiving fentanyl and lorazepam for sedation to maintain acceptable arterial blood gas concentrations. Attempts to reduce the dosages of medication have resulted in life-threatening hypoxia and carbon dioxide retention. Tracheostomy is recommended to prevent permanent vocal cord damage from continued orotracheal intubation. Prior to the operation, no discussions took place concerning tracheostomy placement. She is unmarried, and her only living relative is a sister who resides in another state. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

choices.A: Continue current ventilator support with orotracheal intubation
choices.C: Contact the hospital ethics committee to give consent
choices.D: Discontinue sedation and determine if the patient can communicate her wishes
choices.E: Proceed with tracheostomy as a medical necessity

correctExplanation: Scenarios frequently arise in healthcare in which patients are unable to consent for themselves. For example, patients with altered mental status or who are intubated and sedated lack the capacity to make decisions, which may be caused by the inability to understand the consent process or the inability to vocalize their desires. In this situation, the healthcare provider must receive consent from the patient's health care proxy. While different states have varying laws about the hierarchy of decision-makers, spouses, parents, and siblings are often included. This patient has had ongoing mechanical ventilatory requirements, and she is unlikely to wean from the mechanical ventilator soon given her recurrent hypoxia and hypercarbia. Prolonged orotracheal intubation can lead to laryngeal edema, tracheal stenosis, and oropharyngeal ulcers, whereas the placement of a tracheostomy improves patient comfort, allows them to communicate, and facilitates the ventilator weaning process. Thus, it would be in this patient's best interest to undergo tracheostomy placement. As her wishes are unknown, the most appropriate next step in management would be to reach out to her next of kin, in this case her sister, to obtain consent for the procedure.
